turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, okay. What about specials, are they a trick to get rid of old stock?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sometimes, but usually they're seasonal ingredients the chef is excited about. If the special is fish on a Monday, I'd be a bit more cautious.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why Monday?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many fish markets are closed on Sundays, so Monday fish might be a few days old. It's not a rule, just a hint.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I complain about my food without being awkward?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep it calm and specific. Something like, my steak is quite a bit more cooked than I asked for, could it be redone?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I wait until the end of the meal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No, mention it right away. If you wait, they can't fix it and it looks like you just want money off.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if the waiter gets annoyed?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most won't, kitchens would rather know. If they do get defensive, you can politely ask for a manager.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friends always say / I'm being dramatic when I send things back.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sending back a dish that's wrong isn't dramatic. Being rude about it would be, and you clearly aren't planning to.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you help me figure out a gluten free dinner spot? My roommate just got diagnosed with celiac.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sure. The key is finding places that understand cross contamination, not just ones with a gluten free label on a few dishes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How would I even know that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Call and ask whether they use a separate fryer and prep area. A confident, detailed answer is a really good sign.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What kinds of food are usually safe?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Thai, Mexican and Indian often have lots of naturally gluten free dishes, think rice, corn tortillas and lentils. Still ask about sauces though, soy sauce has wheat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh no, she loves soy sauce.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There's tamari, which is a wheat free version. Lots of Japanese places keep it if you ask.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's such a relief, / she thought sushi was off the table forever.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not at all. Just mention celiac when booking, so the kitchen can be careful.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Booking for tonight. Do restaurants actually keep the table if I'm late?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually for about fifteen minutes. After that, on a busy night, they may give it away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I just call and say I'm running late?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That makes a huge difference. Most places will hold the table longer if they know you're coming.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. And if I cancel last minute, will they charge me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some do, especially if they took your card when you booked. Check the confirmation email for a cancellation policy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I didn't even read that email, honestly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Worth a quick look. It'll also tell you if there's a time limit on the table, some places give you two hours and that's it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why are restaurant wines so expensive?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Restaurants usually mark wine up two or three times what it costs in a shop. It helps pay for glassware, storage and staff.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So is the cheapest bottle a bad deal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often the second cheapest gets the biggest markup, because people avoid looking cheap. The cheapest one can actually be decent value.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's sneaky. What about house wine?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: House wine is usually picked to be easy drinking and fairly priced. It's a safe choice if you don't know the list.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And can I / bring my own bottle?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some places allow it and charge a corkage fee. Call ahead, and don't bring something they already have on their list.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to take my nephew somewhere fun for his eighth birthday.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fun idea. Kids that age usually love places with something to watch, like a teppanyaki grill where the chef cooks at the table.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, the flipping shrimp thing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly, and the onion volcano. Kids tend to talk about it for weeks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it too pricey though?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sometimes, yes. A lunch set is often much cheaper than dinner and has the same show.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hmm, and what if he's a picky eater?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Chicken, rice and noodles are always on the grill, so even picky kids find something. Ask them to skip the spicy sauce for him.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Great, I'll look for one near the mall.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good thinking, then you can add a movie or an ice cream afterwards.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Quick one. What's a good way to find decent restaurants in a small town?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look for places with lots of locals and work trucks parked outside at lunch. They know where the good food is.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, that's a classic.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It works. Also check the bakery, small town bakeries are often the hidden gems.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if there's literally just one diner?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then order what's on the chalkboard. The handwritten specials are usually what the cook actually enjoys making.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm passing through / some tiny places next week on a road trip.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you'll get plenty of chances. Ask the person at the gas station, they always have an opinion.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm going to a really fancy restaurant for the first time and I'm scared of looking stupid.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's completely understandable, but the staff at good places want you to feel comfortable. You can ask them anything.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about all the forks?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start from the outside and work your way in with each course. If you get it wrong, honestly nobody cares.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the dress code?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check their website. If it says smart casual, a nice shirt and clean shoes are enough.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I don't understand / half the menu?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Just ask the waiter to explain a dish. They describe things all night, it's part of the fun.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I order the tasting menu?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If it fits your budget, yes. It takes the decisions away and you get to try the best of the kitchen.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm picking a place for my team dinner on Friday, can you help?
options: The first one is an Italian place downtown, great pasta, but it's quite noisy on weekends.
Then there's a sushi restaurant near the office with private rooms, but it's pretty expensive.
And the last one is a casual barbecue joint with long picnic tables and a big patio.
moshi_comment: For a team dinner, the sushi place's private rooms are a big plus, everyone can talk without shouting. The barbecue joint is cheaper and more relaxed if the weather is nice. What's the budget per person?
I'd lean toward the barbecue place, long tables are perfect for a group and the vibe is easygoing. The Italian spot sounds tasty, but noise on a Friday could make conversation hard.

option_sets.lead_in: My sister's birthday dinner is next week, and I have to choose where we go.
options: First, there's a rooftop bar with small plates and an amazing view of the river.
Second, a family-run Mexican restaurant where the staff sing to you on your birthday.
There's also a fancy French bistro she's mentioned wanting to try for ages.
Or lastly, we could just do a pizza night at my place with the whole family.
moshi_comment: If she's been wanting to try the French bistro for ages, that would feel really thoughtful. The Mexican place is more fun if she enjoys a bit of attention. Does she like being the center of attention?
The rooftop bar sounds special, but small plates can leave people hungry at a birthday dinner. I'd pick the French bistro, and save pizza night for a relaxed family weekend.

option_sets.lead_in: My in-laws are coming for one night only and I've got three restaurants in mind, help me pick.
options: There's a steakhouse by the station with big booths, but the menu barely has anything for my vegetarian sister-in-law.
Then a dim sum place that's lively and cheap, though you have to queue without a booking.
Or a quiet countryside pub about twenty minutes' drive away, with a fireplace and a roast every night.
moshi_comment: The steakhouse is out if your sister-in-law would be stuck with a side salad. Dim sum is fun and everyone shares, but queuing with in-laws is risky. I'd book the countryside pub, as long as someone's happy to drive.

For one special night, I'd lean toward the pub, a fireplace and a roast is hard to fault. Dim sum is the cheaper, livelier option if your in-laws like a buzz. Is anyone in the group sensitive to noise?

option_sets.lead_in: Me and three friends are doing a food crawl downtown and we can only fit in one dinner stop. Which?
options: A tiny taco stand with only stools outside, cash only, but the reviews are ridiculous.
A new Korean fried chicken spot that just opened, apparently the lines are long on Fridays.
A classic old diner that's been there for fifty years, famous for its pie.
Or a fancy small plates bar where everything costs about twelve dollars a plate.
moshi_comment: On a food crawl you want something quick and memorable, so the taco stand is a strong pick, just bring cash. The Korean chicken is great for sharing if the line isn't too bad. I'd save the diner for the dessert leg, that pie sounds like a finale.

The small plates bar will drain your budget fast when you're hungry. I'd go tacos or the fried chicken, both are perfect for grazing. Are you doing a separate dessert stop? If not, the diner and its pie might win.

option_sets.lead_in: I can't decide where to have my thirtieth birthday dinner.
options: There's a rooftop place with fairy lights, but if it rains we get stuck inside a cramped little room.
Then my favorite Italian, where I've been going since I was a teenager and they know my name.
Or a karaoke restaurant with private rooms, the food is just okay but it's a guaranteed party.
moshi_comment: If you want the night to feel personal, the Italian place where they know you is lovely and low risk. The karaoke rooms win if you want a party more than a meal. The rooftop is a gamble unless the forecast looks good.
Thirty is a big one. I'd do dinner at your Italian place and then head out for karaoke afterwards, best of both. The rooftop only makes sense in a dry, warm month. When is your birthday?
